statement: In people who use classic psychedelics, feeling safe and supported is associated with fewer reported difficulties in retrospective surveys, while the only prospective study among these sources found only a weak, uncertain link for the place and the people. In that study (Haijen et al., 2018; about 198 self-selected adults who planned an experience on their own initiative), a good feeling about the people who would be present and about the place, rated within the day before, went with slightly lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores rated about a day after (standardized beta −0.14, p = 0.070, not statistically significant), and with slightly higher well-being two weeks later (1.2 points on the well-being scale per standard deviation of the rating, p = 0.037, one of many coefficients in a model without correction for multiple tests; not significant at four weeks, p = 0.077); a retreat or a setting designed for therapy, reported afterwards in two yes-or-no questions that the authors combined into one variable, showed no statistically significant association with any acute measure (0.02), and the authors note that the term was not defined for participants. In an international online survey of 6,877 self-selected people who had drunk ayahuasca, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety at their last ceremony went with 0.29 points less extreme fear or panic on a 0-to-10 scale (95% CI 0.15 to 0.43, editors' calculation), slightly fewer difficulties in the weeks after, and current distress lower by 0.62 points on the 40-point Kessler scale, under 2 points across the whole rating (editors' arithmetic), after adjustment for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink and for the motivation, ceremony and other support variables; the ratings were made looking back by the same people, and averaged near the top of the scale (Perkins et al., 2021). Among 613 US adults in an online panel who had used a classic psychedelic, those who blamed a lack of psychological support for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.25) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.42, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any); blaming a disagreeable physical environment went with a smaller difference in challenge (0.09) and no detectable difference in harm thoughts, and blaming the people around with no statistically significant difference in either (odds ratio for harm thoughts 0.33, 0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051, lower if anything) (Simonsson et al., 2023). Among 163 experienced people recalling two experiences, mostly at home or at a friend's house, those whose experience was at a party, club or festival (24 first and 12 most recent experiences) had higher average challenge scores than the rest (19 against 17 and 31 against 16 per cent of the maximum), a comparison the authors did not test (Palmer and Maynard, 2022). No study compared settings by design. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In surveys, people who felt safe and supported during a trip reported a little less fear and fewer difficulties, but they rated both afterwards. The only study among these that asked people beforehand found only a weak, uncertain link between feeling good about the place and the people and how the trip went, and no detectable difference for retreats or settings designed for therapy. No study put people in different settings on purpose to compare them.
population: People who use classic psychedelics outside laboratories: adults who planned an experience on their own initiative (one prospective study), people who drink ayahuasca (one international survey), a US online panel and a self-selected survey of experienced people
exposure: The place and the people: feelings about the setting rated the day before; a retreat or therapeutic setting; support and safety at an ayahuasca ceremony rated afterwards; lack of support, a disagreeable place or disagreeable company blamed for the most challenging experience; party, club or festival settings
comparator: People who rated the setting less favourably, did not blame it, or used elsewhere, within each study
outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), extreme fear or panic, difficulties in the weeks after, thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others, and current distress (Kessler-10)
magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018): setting component and challenging experience beta −0.14 (p = 0.070); setting component and well-being at two weeks 1.2 points per standard deviation (p = 0.037; at four weeks p = 0.077); retreat or therapeutic setting 0.02 (p = 0.81). Perkins et al. (2021), per point of a 1-to-4 support-and-safety rating: extreme fear (0 to 10) −0.29 (95% CI −0.43 to −0.15, editors'), integration difficulties −0.13, Kessler-10 −0.62 (under 2 points across the whole rating); the paper does not say which outcomes were modelled as ordinal, so reading −0.29 as points on the fear item assumes a linear model. Simonsson et al. (2023), attributions of the most challenging experience, adjusted only for the other attributions: no support beta 0.25, harm thoughts or attempts OR 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42); disagreeable physical environment 0.09, OR 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35); disagreeable social environment not associated, OR 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051). Palmer and Maynard (2022), untested: party settings 19.27 against 16.77 (first) and 31.46 against 16.16 (most recent) per cent of the maximum CEQ score.

risk_of_bias.note: Retrospective ratings or attributions made by the same people at the same sitting as the outcome, in self-selected samples, with little or no adjustment (very high risk: sc_perkins_2021, sc_simonsson_2023, sc_palmer_2022); the prospective study is at high risk (confounding, heavy attrition) and its retreat item was undefined (sc_haijen_2018).

inconsistency.note: The direction differs by aspect: support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys, but blaming the people around showed no association with challenge (and, if anything, lower odds of harm thoughts) in the panel survey; in the prospective study the setting rating showed only a non-significant trend in the same direction, and a retreat or therapeutic setting no association.

indirectness.note: Worded for the people and settings studied.

imprecision.note: Large surveys; the prospective coefficient's interval includes zero, which the statement says.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, giving very low (the floor). Status mixed: four independent studies; support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys (Perkins et al.; the no-support attribution in Simonsson et al.) and the untested party comparison points the same way, but blaming the people around showed no such link, and the one prospective study found only a non-significant trend for its setting rating (and a weak link with well-being two weeks later) and no association for a retreat or therapeutic setting; recall at the same sitting may explain part of the difference, but no study has shown that it does.
